title: Mentor chat with Dana
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex asks mentor Dana whether to leave an in-house insurance job for a small exhibit design studio, they work through salary negotiation and imposter syndrome, Dana recommends a book, and Alex's request to discuss portfolio reviews is never picked up.

utterances.text: Okay, you said on the phone it was urgent-ish. What's going on?
So, the studio I told you about, the one that designs museum exhibits? They made me an offer yesterday.
Alex! That's huge. Congratulations.
Thanks. I think. I've been staring at the email for a day and I can't decide if I'm thrilled or terrified.
Probably both. Walk me through it. What's pulling you there?

The work, mostly. They're doing the new gallery at the science center, all the interactive panels and wayfinding. It's the kind of thing I wanted to do when I got into design. Right now I'm redesigning claim forms for the fourth time.
And what's keeping you at the insurance company?
Honestly? Stability. Good benefits. I know everyone. And the studio is twelve people, so if they lose one big contract, I'm worried I'm the first to go.
That's a fair worry. Did you ask them about their pipeline?
No. Should I?
Absolutely. Ask how many projects they have booked for next year and how long their longest client has stayed. A good studio will just tell you.
Okay, that's a good one. Oh, and remind me to ask you about portfolio reviews at some point, because they want me to present at the final meeting too.
Sure. So what about the money? That's usually where these things get stuck.
Yeah. It's about eight thousand less than I make now.
Did you push back?
I said thank you and that I'd think about it. I didn't want to seem ungrateful.
Okay, that's the first thing I want to fix. Asking isn't ungrateful. They already decided they want you. That's the moment you have the most leverage you'll ever have there.
But what if they just pull the offer?
A reasonable company does not pull an offer because you asked a polite question. In ten years, I've never seen it happen.
Okay. So what do I actually say?
Lead with excitement, then a specific number. Something like, I'm really excited about this role, and to make it work I'd need the base to be closer to what I make now. And then you stop talking.
Stop talking is the part I'm bad at.
Everyone is. Let the silence sit. And if they can't move on salary, ask about other things. Extra vacation days, a training budget, a review at six months instead of a year.
I didn't even think about a six-month review.
There's a book I give everyone in your spot. Never Split the Difference, by Chris Voss. He was an FBI hostage negotiator.
Hostage negotiator? For a salary talk?
Ha, I know. But the ideas are about listening and asking open questions, not tricking people. It'll make you way less nervous.
Okay, I'll grab it this weekend. Can I tell you the real thing, though?
Of course.
I don't think I'm qualified. I've never designed anything physical. Everything I've done lives on a screen. I keep waiting for them to realize they picked the wrong person.
Ah. The imposter thing.
Yeah. Is that dumb?
Not dumb at all. I felt that way at every job I've ever started, including the one I'm in now. But think about it. They saw your work, they interviewed you three times, and they still picked you.
I guess. It still feels like I fooled them.
You can't fool a room of twelve designers for three interviews. What they're hiring is how you think about people moving through information. That transfers from a claim form to a gallery wall.
Huh. I never thought of it like that.
And feeling out of your depth is usually a sign you picked something that'll make you grow. The danger is the job where you feel totally comfortable for five years.
That's basically my current job.
There you go. So, here's your homework. Ask about the pipeline, counter with a number, read the book. Then decide.
Okay. Pipeline, number, book. Thank you, Dana. Really.
Anytime. Let me know what they say.
